title: Win as a team, lose as a team
principle: No one wins or loses a game alone. Every player, the coaches and the people in the stands are part of the result.
life_lesson: Families, classrooms and workplaces work the same way: you share the credit and you share the load.
for_player: One at-bat or one error never decides a game by itself. Pick up your teammates the way you want them to pick you up.
for_coach: Talk about results as 'we'. Never single out the player who made the last out or the last error.
for_parent: Celebrate the team first. After a loss, don't let your child carry it alone or put it on a teammate.
for_umpire: The crew works as a team too, and their calls are part of the game, never the reason a team lost.

title: Everyone makes mistakes: forgive others, own yours
principle: Players, coaches, parents and umpires are all human, and we all make mistakes. Forgive the mistakes of others, and take responsibility for your own so you can learn from them and grow. We strive to be perfect, but nobody is.
life_lesson: Owning a mistake and learning from it is a habit that lasts far beyond the diamond.
for_player: Say 'that's on me', then ask what you'd do differently next time. When a teammate makes a mistake, let it go and pick them up.
for_coach: Model it: own your own coaching mistakes out loud, and treat a player's error as a teaching moment, not a punishment.
for_parent: Show your child how to own a mistake without beating themselves up, and never blame the umpire, the coach or a teammate in front of them.
for_umpire: Umpires miss calls too. Owning that calmly earns respect; everyone else should give the same grace.

title: Believe in your players before they believe in themselves
principle: Have confidence in your players even when they don't show it, even when their track record says failure. Don't lose that confidence. Feed it to them and they will succeed.
life_lesson: People rise to the belief others show in them, at school, at work and at home.
for_player: Your coach picked you for this moment because they believe you can do it. Trust your preparation.
for_coach: Give players the chance to step up, including the ones without a great record yet, and tell them you believe in them before the result.
for_parent: Your belief matters most when your child is struggling. Tell them you love watching them play, hit or no hit.

title: Winning comes from a winning formula
principle: Winning is fun and feels great, but it doesn't happen without a winning formula: healthy arms, many players who can contribute, and everyone playing their part. Don't put the scoreboard above developing players.
life_lesson: Long-term success comes from building people and habits, not from chasing one result at any cost.
for_player: Do your job, whatever your role is that day. A team of players doing their part beats one star.
for_coach: Protect arms and build depth: give more pitchers reps in lower-pressure innings so they're ready when you need them. Rest your best arm when the rules or their body say so.
for_parent: Measure the season by how your child grows and how the team plays together, not only by wins.

title: Big moments aren't scripted
principle: The moments that matter most aren't planned. They happen because kids are put in situations where they can fail or succeed, and sometimes they succeed through what could have been failure.
life_lesson: You can't plan for every opportunity, but you can be ready for it and willing to take it.
for_player: Play every pitch to the end and be ready: your moment can come when you least expect it.
for_coach: Put kids in situations where they can fail or succeed. That's where growth and team belief come from.
for_parent: Let your child take on hard moments. The chance to fail is also the chance to shine.

title: Believe in your teammates, especially when they fail
principle: Believe in your teammates, especially when they fail. The moment after a mistake is when a teammate needs your belief most.
life_lesson: Standing by people when they stumble is what makes a team, a family or a group of friends strong.
for_player: After a teammate's error or strikeout, be the first to say 'next one's yours'. Never roll your eyes or turn away.
for_coach: Teach players how to pick each other up, and praise it when you see it, as much as you praise a hit.
for_parent: Cheer for every player on the team, especially the one who's struggling, and teach your child to do the same.

title: Your value isn't your stat line
principle: Your value is not determined by your failures or your successes.
life_lesson: Who you are matters more than any result: a grade, a game or a job outcome doesn't define your worth.
for_player: A strikeout or a home run doesn't change who you are. Show up, compete and be a good teammate.
for_coach: Make sure every player knows their place on the team doesn't depend on today's box score.
for_parent: Love your child the same after an 0-for-4 as after a 3-for-4, and let them see it.
for_umpire: One missed call doesn't define an umpire either.

title: A game built on failure
principle: In baseball, succeeding about 30% of the time at the plate can make a Hall of Fame career at the professional level. That's a 70% failure rate. You will not win every competition, and you will not lose every competition, but you will learn and grow through every competition.
life_lesson: Failing often on the way to success is normal in anything worth doing; what matters is learning from each try.
for_player: Expect to fail more than you succeed at the plate, even when you're good. Judge yourself by your approach and effort, then go again.
for_coach: Help players keep failure in perspective: celebrate good at-bats and hard effort, not just hits.
for_parent: Remind your child that even the best hitters fail most of the time. A tough day is part of the game, not a sign they don't belong.

title: Today's opponents, tomorrow's teammates
principle: Your opponents today may be your teammates in the future. Treat them that way, especially after a game. As competitive athletes in the same sport, you are all brothers and sisters.
life_lesson: Respect for competitors builds the relationships and reputation you carry for the rest of your life.
for_player: Compete hard, then shake hands like you mean it. Congratulate a good play by the other team.
for_coach: Model respect for the other team and its coaches, and expect it of your players in the handshake line.
for_parent: Cheer for good plays by both teams and speak well of opponents in front of your child. The other team's kids are someone's children too.
for_umpire: Treat both teams the same; respect for everyone on the field starts with the crew.

title: Control the moment
principle: When a play gets loud and confusing, the adults set the temperature. Umpires stop the play, get together and explain calmly; coaches lower their voices and wait for the explanation.
life_lesson: In any heated moment, slowing down and getting the facts straight before reacting keeps a mistake from turning into a fight.
for_player: When the umpire calls time, stop and listen. Don't keep running or tagging because someone is yelling.
for_coach: Yelling directions during a confusing play makes it harder for everyone, including your players. Wait for the umpires, then ask calmly what rule applies.
for_parent: Stay in the stands and stay calm. The players take their cue from the adults.
for_umpire: Kill it loudly: 'Time! Dead ball!' with both arms up. Get your partner, agree on what happened and where everyone goes, then explain once to each coach. Don't let the volume change the call: a misapplied rule can be corrected, and a judgment call stands.

title: Play until you hear 'foul'
principle: Every batted ball is live until the umpire says otherwise. Players don't decide fair or foul; the umpire does. So run hard and play the ball until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'
life_lesson: Don't quit on something because you've already decided how it will turn out. Finish the job, and leave the call to the person whose call it is.
for_player: Hit it, drop the bat and run, every time, until you hear 'Foul!'. Fielders: if the ball is in play, make the play.
for_coach: Teach 'run until you hear foul' at practice with rollers that go foul and come back fair. During a play, one short word ('Run!') helps more than a dozen shouted directions.
for_parent: If your player stood and watched, make it a learning moment on the ride home, not a criticism. 'Run until you hear foul' is a rule many players learn the hard way.
for_umpire: Make the fair signal big and immediate: point toward fair territory as soon as the ball is touched or stops in fair territory. Call 'Foul!' loudly with both arms up. Clear signals stop the guessing and the yelling.
